Article Title: 'We hear you': Rahul Gandhi's message to traders in Delhi amid anti-CEC stir
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Monday expressed solidarity with Delhi traders, alleging that the government had disrupted business by shutting metro services, sealing roads and locking down the capital. Linking the restrictions to his allegations of “vote chori”, Rahul demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi sack Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, whom he referred to as “Accused No. 4”."To every trader in Delhi: We love you and hear you. The Govt shut the metro, sealed our roads and locked down our capital. With a stolen vote nothing is safe - your shop, your savings, your children’s future. Tell Modi to sack accused no. 4, Gyanesh Kumar and the protests will stop in 30 seconds."This comes after traders had earlier urged the LoP and congress party to stop their protests citing business losses as they're forced to shutdown their businesses amid protests. Recently, the Chamber of Trade and Industry on Saturday urged Rahul to postpone the INDIA bloc's upcoming rally on November 1 at Ramlila Maidan, saying the demonstration could disrupt business worth Rs 10,000 crore during the peak Diwali shopping season."This year, Dhanteras falls on Friday, November 6, Diwali on November 8 and Bhai Dooj on November 10. People begin shopping for Dhanteras and Diwali a week in advance. In Delhi alone, Dhanteras-related business across sectors such as gold and silver, utensils, electronics, textiles, dry fruits, sweets, automobiles, vehicles, property and gift items amounts to approximately Rs 25,000 crore. This trade is the backbone of Delhi's economy," the letter reads.The traders’ body said markets typically witness a surge in activity about a week before festivals, raising concerns over the timing of the rally. Goyal added that traders in Delhi had already incurred losses of around Rs 3,000 crore in October due to rallies, marches and road closures in Connaught Place, India Gate and central Delhi.

He alleged that the government had disrupted business by shutting metro services, sealing roads and locking down the capital. Rahul demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi sack Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, whom he referred to as 'Accused No. 4'

Article Title: Australia expands biometric requirements for visa applicants in India from October 26
Article Text:
Australia introduces fingerprint and facial image requirements for certain new visa applications from India, effective Oct 26

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Australian government on Monday expanded biometric collection requirements for visa applicants in India from October 26, introducing fingerprint and facial image collection for certain new visa applications.The change covers applications filed on or after that date, while those submitted earlier and visas already issued remain unaffected, the Australian high commission said. The department of home affairs will inform applicants who need to complete the additional step and explain how to do so.Applicants may be directed to one of 16 biometric collection centres operated by VFS Global across India. Those who meet the eligibility criteria may instead be able to submit their biometrics through the Australian Immi App.The government said the move is intended to make identity checks more reliable, curb fraud and protect applicants from identity misuse. Australia already collects biometric data from visa applicants in nearly 60 countries, and the extension brings India into the programme.Visa processing times are not expected to be adversely affected if applicants provide their biometrics promptly after being notified.Applicants have been advised not to book an appointment or use the app until they receive an official notification from the department of home affairs.The Australian government said applicants’ personal information would be handled under relevant laws and transferred through encrypted channels.It also clarified that buying optional services from service providers would not affect either processing times or visa decisions.
Article Summary: The Australian government on Monday expanded biometric collection requirements for visa applicants in India from October 26. The change covers applications filed on or after that date, while those submitted earlier and visas already issued remain unaffected. The government said the move is intended to make identity checks more reliable, curb fraud and protect applicants.

Article Title: EAM to UN: Lead during global crises, don’t just be a spectator
Article Text:
Jaishankar urges UN to show leadership during global crises, says large parts of the world can't be left out of decision-making.

NEW DELHI: Urging UN to show leadership, and not remain a mere spectator to global crises, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said Sunday large parts of the world cannot be left out from decision-making. At an event on UN Day, he underlined the need for long-awaited reforms.“We live in an imperfect world but we all continuously strive towards greater perfection. Where UN is concerned, that means recognising its shortcomings and limitations and seeking its improvement. The case for reformed multilateralism gets stronger by the day,” he said.Jaishankar spoke about how countries with little say were paying the price for conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine. He also underscored the threat to peace from terrorism, saying its usage as an instrument of statecraft is simply unacceptable.“It can never be justified; it can never be rationalised. Yet, it continues because not all states really display zero-tolerance. Despite history holding so many lessons, some still allow political calculations to take precedence.”“The world must develop sharper awareness about this common threat.And it must come together with stronger resolve and counter terrorism in all its forms and manifestations,” he added.He said the world cannot advance half-prosperous and half-denied and in an era of intricate supply chains, of globalised markets and of common resources, this is simply a prescription for continuous instability.“The Global South today faces a 4F crisis: of finance, fuel, food, and fertiliser. The Global North must realise it has equal stakes in finding solutions. International economy must be urgently de-risked and nations provided with more diversified options. Market distortions through constriction and choke-points only add to suffering. A genuine dialogue in this regard is overdue,” the minister said.Underlining the significance of AI as the mother of all change, Jaishankar said something so sweeping and consequential cannot be left in the hands of just a few. “That would go counter to the trends of freedom and democratisation that the world has seen over the last eighty years,” he added.
Article Summary: Jaishankar spoke about how countries with little say were paying the price for conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine. He underscored the threat to peace from terrorism, saying its usage as an instrument of statecraft is simply unacceptable. He said the world cannot advance half-prosperous and half-denied in an era of intricate supply chains.

Article Title: Massive fire engulfs Shiv Market near Jammu Railway Station, 35-40 shops gutted
Article Text:
Massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station

NEW DELHI: Around 35 to 40 shops were completely gutted after a massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station, in the early hours of Monday. No casualties or injuries have been reported so far, while fire and emergency services teams were working to bring the blaze under control. The cause of the fire remains unknown.BJP MLA Vikram Randhawa said the fire reportedly began due to a short circuit in one shop before spreading rapidly to adjoining establishments. Shiv Market is a major commercial hub with shops selling dry fruits and blankets, as well as eateries and dhabas.“The fire started with a short circuit in one shop and spread rapidly, engulfing surrounding shops. By the time the fire brigade arrived, the entire market had been consumed by the flames. In my estimation, about 35 to 40 shops have been completely gutted,” Randhawa said.Describing the firefighting efforts, the MLA said the blaze had engulfed the entire market by the time the situation could be brought under control. He added that police personnel and senior officers were actively involved in managing the situation.“As it kept growing, by the time the whole system came under control, it had already engulfed the entire market.Right now, our police are completely alert and actively controlling the situation. You can see that from the SHO to our SP, everyone is personally involved, even holding and dragging pipes all the way to the shops,” Randhawa said.A shopkeeper said at least 25 to 30 shops had suffered total losses and urged the administration to provide compensation to those affected.“The entire market has been reduced to ashes. At least 25 to 30 shops are a total loss. We pray to God to grant everyone the strength to cope with this — the loss is immense, a total loss. I also urge the administration to step in as quickly as possible and ensure that compensation is provided without delay,” the shopkeeper said.Randhawa said the full extent of the damage could be assessed only after the situation was completely under control. He said shopkeepers were cooperating with the administration, with the deputy commissioner, SP South, DSP, SHO and their teams present at the site. Members of civil society were also helping with relief efforts.On compensation for affected shopkeepers, Randhawa said the matter would be discussed with the administration later, describing the damage as massive.
Article Summary: A massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station, in the early hours of Monday. Shiv Market is a major commercial hub with shops selling dry fruits and blankets. No casualties or injuries have been reported so far, while fire and emergency services teams are working to bring the blaze under control.

Article Title: AI model uses face photos to estimate biological age, predict survival risk in cancer patients
Article Text:
Patients in the highest AI-assessed risk group had more than three times the mortality risk of those in the lowest-risk group, study finds

NEW DELHI:

The Lancet Digital Health

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A photograph of the face could one day help doctors assess how old a person appears biologically and estimate survival risk in cancer patients, according to a new artificial intelligence (AI) model developed by researchers and tested in separate groups of patients.The model, called Foundation Artificial Intelligence for Health Recognition-Face (FAHR-Face), was trained on more than 40 million facial photographs and adapted for two tasks — estimating biological age, or how old a person appears to be physically, and predicting the risk of death. The findings were published inin 2026.When tested on publicly available photographs, the AI model estimated biological age with an average error of about five years. Among 38,183 patients treated at six US centres affiliated with Harvard, those who appeared biologically older than their actual age tended to have poorer survival outcomes.A second AI model, FAHR-FaceSurvival, was trained on photographs of 34,363 cancer patients and tested on another 3,820. Patients classified in the highest-risk group were more than three times as likely to die as those in the lowest-risk group, even after researchers accounted for other factors, including patients’ clinical characteristics and demographic details.The researchers also tested the models on 4,892 cancer patients treated in the Netherlands. The results suggested that the AI could help estimate survival risk in patients beyond the original US group.Dr Mandeep Singh Malhotra, director of surgical oncology at the CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said the approach was an interesting development, but its reliability in India needed to be established.“An important consideration is whether this facial recognition AI can deliver equally reliable results in the Indian population, given our distinct epidemiological profile and diverse facial features. This remains to be established,” he said.Malhotra said the technology could eventually complement precision oncology if combined with genomic testing and other diagnostic techniques, including liquid biopsy. Such an approach, he said, could potentially improve predictions of cancer survival, help detect recurrence earlier and enable timely intervention.“Rather than viewing it as a standalone technique, its potential may lie in complementing established diagnostic approaches, including genomics and liquid biopsy, as part of a more comprehensive, personalised approach to cancer care,” he said.The two AI models appeared to identify different aspects of health-related information from facial photographs. Using them together improved the accuracy of survival-risk estimates, suggesting that facial analysis could eventually complement existing tools doctors use to assess patients and plan treatment.However, the model cannot diagnose cancer or predict an individual’s lifespan. Since the study mainly involved patients in the US and the Netherlands, its findings may not apply to other populations. Lighting, image quality and facial expressions may also affect estimates. Further validation is needed before the technology can be used routinely in clinical practice.
Article Summary: The model, called Foundation Artificial Intelligence for Health Recognition-Face (FAHR-Face), was trained on more than 40 million facial photographs. It was adapted for two tasks — estimating biological age, or how old a person appears to be physically, and predicting the risk of death.

Article Title: Former CJI D Y Chandrachud was more deferential to government than needed, says Justice Kaul
Article Text:
Former SC judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul alleges in his book that ex-CJI D Y Chandrachud was overly deferential to the government on judicial appointments

‘DYC asked if he should call government on collegium picks’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former CJI D Y Chandrachud was more deferential to the govt than necessary in matters of judicial appointments, former SC judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has said in his forthcoming book ‘Without Fear Or Favour’, and claimed that he was prevented from hearing petitions for re-examination of the validity of provisions of PMLA.Kaul also claimed Justice Chandrachud had, allegedly under pressure from govt, withdrawn a case from him in which a bench headed by him had questioned delays in implementation of the SC collegium’s resolutions for appointment of judges. This, he said, “troubled him the most” as the case was assigned years ago and was taken away all of a sudden.Reacting to the claims, Justice Chandrachud said, “There was never even a dissent by any member of the collegium over any name during discussions for appointments to the SC.”Sources said resolutions passed by the collegium for appointments to the SC during Justice Chandrachud’s tenure were unanimous and signed by all members of the collegium without recording a single dissent.In this case, a bench of Justices Kaul and Sudhanshu Dhulia had pulled up govt for its alleged pick-and-choose policy in clearing names sent by the collegium and had on Nov 20, 2023, asked why Centre was not transferring four judges from Gujarat HC and not appointing two Sikh lawyers for Punjab and Haryana HC as recommended by the collegium.The case was thereafter taken away from his bench and it has not been listed in the last three years.In an interview to Karan Thapar for The Wire, Justice Kaul claimed the former CJI took him aside during a collegium meeting and asked whether he should telephone govt to ascertain its views on the proposed appointments. Justice Kaul said pre-approval from govt before discussions in the collegium was a matter of concern.“This has unfortunately become a practice of names being discussed, and some kind of previous discussion with govt. That used to happen. It has been happening, I think before CJI Chandrachud and after. That is why it troubles me,” he said, adding that there was nothing wrong in holding consultations with govt, but it should happen only after the collegium’s decision and not before.Asked whether Justice Chandrachud was too deferential to govt, Justice Kaul said, “There is a judicial side and there is an administrative side of the Chief Justice of India. I wouldn’t be concerned with the judicial side. I believe he had both the intellectual heft and the capacity and hard work to do so. But in consultations with govt and collaboration, I felt he was more deferential than necessary to carry it forward.Justice Kaul said he tried to discourage Justice Chandrachud from discussing everything with govt beforehand as it could create its own problems. Asked whether Justice Chandrachud failed to live up to the high expectations from him, Justice Kaul said, “I would say that expectations were higher from him.”TOI has reported how Justice Kaul had vigorously and successfully pushed many names for judgeship as part of the SC and HC collegiums and three of his proposals had met with resistance from other members of the panel. The then CJI had tactically refrained from holding collegium meetings to avoid embarrassing situations.In reply to the TOI article, Justice Kaul had sent a rejoinder and said, “There was no question of insistence of appointment of those suggested by me and all recommendations have been made by consensus. That other collegium members had reservations and I pushed the names, thus, seem to be a flight of your imagination.”
Article Summary: Ex-CJI D Y Chandrachud was more deferential to the govt than necessary in matters of judicial appointments, former SC judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has said in his forthcoming book ‘Without Fear Or Favour’ Kaul also claimed that he was prevented from hearing petitions for re-examination of the validity of provisions of PMLA.

NEW DELHI: Election Commission has declined to disclose the name and version of the software it used to identify errors and anomalies in voter rolls during SIR, saying the information was related to “commercial confidence, trade secrets and intellectual property” and, thus, exempt under RTI Act. The reply, dated Oct 16, came in response to an RTI plea.M A Mujeeb Ayyub, a social activist from Karimpur in Telangana, in his RTI plea dated July 27 had sought information regarding the software, application, algorithm or AI platform used by EC to identify errors, anomalies or inconsistencies in electoral rolls during SIR.In response, EC said, “No new software has been developed or procured for the SIR exercise. Further, EROs decide on the inclusion/exclusion of an elector on the basis of facts and records.” An EC official said software and algorithm details were conventionally not shared under RTI requests. Even EVM manufacturers like Bharat Electronics Ltd and Electronics Corporation of India Ltd have earlier refused to share EVM source codes while replying to RTI queries.Ayyub had sought to know whether the software or the AI platform automatically flagged records for verification, correction or deletion and if that was the case, what was the detailed workflow followed after such records were identified.He had asked whether any AI, machine learning, predictive analytics, or automated decision support system was used in any stage of the SIR exercise.In response to the queries, EC simply said the information sought was a “clarification which does not come under the information as per Section 2(f) of RTI Act”.

Article Title: EPFO considers Rs 25,000cr war chest to stabilise interest payouts
Article Text:
File photo: Employees Provident Fund Organisation- EPFO

Report on ISR sent to panel studying EPFO investment framework

NEW DELHI: Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation is discussing a dedicated Rs 25,000-crore Interest Stabilisation Reserve, designed to insulate the annual interest payouts of its nearly 30 crore members from the turbulence caused by corporate bond defaults and forced-exit losses.Officials said EPFO and government want a stable regime for its subscribers and wish to avoid any sharp fall or spike in rates due to market conditions or defaults.Under existing regulatory frameworks, credit losses and exit haircuts, resulting from downgraded securities, directly impact EPFO’s interest account and depress the annual interest rate for members.A proposal submitted by IIM Kozhikode, which among other things studied the feasibility of creating an Interest Stabilisation Reserve (ISR), was discussed in detail by EPFO’s investment committee (IC) Thursday, TOI has learnt.The report has now been sent to a high-poweredJ panel constituted to examine the agency’s investment framework and recognise non-performing investments.The report suggested building the stabilisation reserve progressively via surplus ETF capital gains and excess interest income and investing it strictly in liquid govt securities (G-Secs) to ensure absolute capital safety, sovereign backing, immediate liquidity, and risk-free yield, said persons familiar with the deliberations.The reserve will not only shield subscribers but will also back active exit policies and empower portfolio managers to execute disciplined, multi-year exits from troubled assets without hesitation.The report took into account the current realities of India’s over-the-counter (OTC) corporate bond market, which remains shallow and illiquid, such that when institutional holders such as EPFO are forced to exit distressed assets, thin market depth results in severe haircuts.Historically, EPFO relied heavily on equity ETF capital gains to offset credit stress.The report, however, noted that the volatile market downturn of FY 2019-20 coincided with major credit events like the IL&FS default, which exposed a critical vulnerability.“Credit stress and equity market crashes are highly correlated. Relying solely on ETF gains is dangerous; a standalone prudential reserve is a structural necessity,” it said.The study evaluated absolute worst-case liquidation scenarios across the portfolio netted against available ETF gains, pinpointing a cumulative baseline shortfall of approximately Rs 23,837 crore.“To account for incomplete market data and ensure a bulletproof prudential buffer, the report recommends formalising an ISR Fund of Rs 25,000 crore,” it said.The study also ran a historical back-testing simulation which modelled portfolio returns from 2010-11 to 2023-24, demonstrating that a Rs 25,000-crore baseline successfully absorbs annual shortfalls and stabilises declared interest rates across typical economic cycles.The only exception was 2019-20, where portfolio deficit spiked to Rs 55,640 crore, leading to deep drawdown from the reserve.“However, the subsequent recovery in investment performance in later years indicates that such a shortfall would likely have been temporary in nature.In such a scenario, EPFO could have bridged the temporary deficit through a short-term advance or loan mechanism, which could subsequently be repaid from future surpluses generated during recovery years,” the study said.
Article Summary: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation is discussing a dedicated Rs 25,000-crore Interest Stabilisation Reserve. The reserve would insulate the annual interest payouts of its nearly 30 crore members from turbulence caused by corporate bond defaults and forced-exit losses.

Article Title: Ahead of leaders' summit, Quad foreign ministers to meet in US
Article Text:
External affairs minister S. Jaishankar (file photo)

Quad foreign ministers will meet this week in Atlanta on the sidelines of a G20 ministerial gathering, official sources confirmed, signalling that that the strategic forum remains resilient despite recent India-US diplomatic turbulence. This will be the second meeting of the grouping—comprising India, the US, Japan, and Australia—this year, after the event India hosted in May.The foreign ministers will look to outline the agenda for the Quad leaders' summit in Manila next month on the margins of ASEAN meetings. External affairs minister S Jaishankar will travel to Atlanta for the G20 and Quad foreign ministers' meetings that US secretary of state Marco Rubio will host on October 30-31.The event in Manila – likely on November 16 - will be the first Quad leaders' summit in 2 years, following the downturn in India-US ties that prevented India from hosting the summit last year. The leaders' summit, which is expected to push forward key initiatives in maritime security and critical supply chain security, will be significant in terms of both its timing and venue.It will take place in the middle of raging maritime tensions between Manila and Beijing, and days before another visit to China by President Donald Trump this year for the APEC summit.Trump is scheduled to travel to Shenzhen from Manila for the summit.The Quad leaders' summit is expected to focus on improving connectivity through resilient infrastructure, cooperation in critical and emerging technologies, maritime security, space and regional and global issues including the ongoing conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine.The G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta will also be important as the last major ministerial gathering of the grouping before the summit on December 14-15 in Miami that will be attended by PM Narendra Modi. It is expected to focus on issues like economic resilience, energy security, AI governance and regional conflicts.In December, apart from the US, Modi is also scheduled to travel to Canada and Belgium with focus on wrapping up trade deals with Ottawa and the EU.Under its stewardship of the intergovernmental forum that includes 19 countries along with the European and African Union, the US has prioritised economic prosperity by limiting regulatory burdens, affordable and secure energy supply chains, and pioneering innovations in AI and emerging technologies.During his visit to India this month, Rubio confirmed that the leaders' summit will take place in the Philippines next month on the margins of ASEAN. A bilateral Trump-Modi meeting is also expected in Manila – the second this year after the meeting on the G7 sidelines in France in June.
Article Summary: Quad foreign ministers will meet this week in Atlanta on the sidelines of a G20 ministerial gathering. This will be the second meeting of the grouping after the event India hosted in May. Foreign ministers will look to outline the agenda for the Quad leaders' summit in Manila next month.

Article Title: ‘Creamy layer case in SC won’t hit seniority of CSE-2025 batch’
Article Text:
File photo: Supreme Court

NEW DELHI: The pendency of the case regarding the OBC creamy layer in Supreme Court will not affect the seniority of successful candidates of 2025 batch even though their service allocation and foundation course are still to be finalised, official sources said on Sunday.DoPT officials said, “The department and all training institutes are prepared to allocate services expeditiously to CSE- 2025 candidates and commence foundation course at the earliest. Delay in commencement of the foundation course will have no bearing on the seniority, gradation or other service conditions of the candidates.”The clarification concerns the fate of successful candidates in the wake of SC’s Rohith Nathan judgement of March 11 in which it had said “salary” cannot be added to “income” for defining “creamy layer” criteria for any category of OBC candidates, including those whose parents are employed in PSUs/banks, etc. The judgement pertained to the case of candidates from PSU background being categorised over the years as “creamy layer” by including “salary” in the “income” of their parents.
Article Summary: The case regarding the OBC creamy layer in Supreme Court will not affect the seniority of successful candidates of 2025 batch. Service allocation and foundation course are still to be finalised, official sources said. DoPT officials said, “The department and all training institutes are prepared to allocate services expeditiously to CSE- 2025 candidates”

Article Title: Raids on NE drug cartels reveal illicit deals worth Rs 270cr
Article Text:
Multi-agency raids in Assam, Mizoram and Manipur exposed over Rs 270 crore in narco-hawala transactions

NEW DELHI: In a major crackdown on cross-border narco-hawala networks in northeastern states, multi-agency search operations by at least 38 teams at 38 locations simultaneously, revealed illicit transactions of over Rs 270 crore, and led to arrest of six people and freezing of over 1,425 mule bank accounts. Properties worth over Rs 26 crore were also frozen or attached during the searches.“Modi govt’s lethal blow against drugs continues... Our agencies launched a barrage of simultaneous crackdowns across 38 locations in Assam, Mizoram and Manipur on Oct 23, smashing an international narco-cartel,” Union home minister Amit Shah said Sunday. Shah said India will hammer until the last nail is driven into the coffin of drug cartels.He also outlined govt’s policy of ‘zero tolerance’ against drugs and the strategic shift from a seizure-centric to a network-centric approach. The drive is part of Centre’s mission to eradicate drug smuggling syndicates by 2029.The latest searches were conducted on several premises in Aizawl, Champhai and Lawngtlai and Churachandpur and were related to cross-border trafficking of heroin, brown sugar and methamphetamine tablets from Myanmar and hawala settlement of drug proceeds. The operation was conducted by ED in coordination with NCB and Mizoram Police.ED has identified layered transactions of over Rs 270 crore, handled by illicit money exchangers, or hawala network, in Champhai, including Rs 125 crore in cash received from Assam, Nagaland, Bengal, Tripura and Delhi.
Article Summary: Multi-agency raids in Assam, Mizoram and Manipur exposed over Rs 270 crore in narco-hawala transactions. Properties worth over Rs 26 crore were also frozen or attached during the searches. The drive is part of Centre’s mission to eradicate drug smuggling syndicates by 2029.

Article Title: Women founders are building India's social startups, their representation in nonprofits outpaces corporate leadership by a big margin, shows study
Article Text:
Women founders are building India's social startups

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A survey of more than 145 organisations working in the social impact space shows that over 57% of non-profits have at least one female founder – more than three times the 18% share reported among Indian startups. Moreover, female representation in the nonprofit sector outpaces corporate leadership, where women hold just 1.8% of CEO positions, 4.4% of CFO positions, and 29% of executive director roles.These findings are part of accelerator for non-profits Change Engine’s ‘East of Doing Good’ report - “Access to flexible funding: a Gender Lens”. The survey covers small organisations (annual budgets less than Rs 1 crore), medium (annual budgets between Rs 1 crore -5 crore) and large organisations (Rs 5 crore and more). The study sample also had an almost equal split between organisations eligible for foreign funding (with FCRA or US 501(c)) and those that were not.Out of the 145 plus organisations surveyed, nearly 31% have only female founders, while around 27% have both male and female founders.The research also shows that women are not only founding more nonprofits, but women founded organisations are better funded and hold more long term flexible funding.The study found that non-profits with atleast one female founder also had bigger budgets. The data shows that 70% of organisations with at least one female founder have an annual budget of over Rs 1 crore, compared to 43.5% of organisations with only-male founders.Also around 21% of organisations with at least one female founder have more than 25% of their budget in flexible unrestricted funding, compared to just about 13% of organisations with only male founders. Flexible funding is the non-programmatic funding that nonprofits can use to invest in talent, technology, research and strengthening the organisation.As far as long-term grants are concerned it turns out that over 65% of organisations with at least one female founder have access to multi-year funding (three years or more), compared to around 56% of organisations with only male founders. Among these, around 27% of organisations with at least one female founder have received multi-year grants above Rs 1 crore, compared to just about 11% of only male founder organisations.The report highlights that when asked to rate (on a scale of 1-5) how easy it was to raise unrestricted funds from corporate social responsibility (CSR), high net-worth individuals (HNIs), domestic foundations, foreign foundations, and crowdfunding/retail, organisations with at least one female founder scored consistently scored higher across every category with an average score of 2.41 in comparison with 2.06 of organisations with only male founders.However, challenges remain. The study shows that cheque sizes remain small for everyone: “A staggering 82% of organisations with at least one female founder and 83% of only male founded organisations said typical unrestricted cheque sizes in India are less than Rs 25 lakh, showing that the small-cheque problem cuts across gender lines,” the study highlights.Varun Aggarwal and Shubham Bansal, co-founders, Change Engine highlighted that the findings show that women are leading India’s social sector and building bigger and better resourced organisations. We need to encourage more women to come into this sector," Aggarwal asserted. “In our accelerator, we meet women founders who are building strong, ambitious institutions to tackle some of India’s biggest social challenges. It’s encouraging to see that what we’ve been observing on the ground is now backed by data. Six in ten nonprofits in our survey were founded by a woman founder,” Bansal added.However, the Change Engine founders highlight that the access to unrestricted flexible funding remains consistently low across the board with 80% of the surveyed founders reporting that they struggle to scale their work due to the lack of unrestricted funding. “This funding rigidity forces organisations to spend disproportionate time on fundraising, rather than focusing on innovation and impact,” they added.
Article Summary: Over 57% of non-profits in India have at least one female founder. This is more than three times the 18% share reported among Indian startups. Female representation in the nonprofit sector outpaces corporate leadership. Women founded organisations are better funded and hold more long term flexible funding.

Article Title: Indian American physician Navin Shah commits $525,000 to infectious disease program in Pune
Article Text:
The five-year initiative, established in collaboration with

Johns Hopkins University

, will support research, medical training, faculty exchanges and patient care at BJ Government Medical College.

Expanding research and patient care

Decades-long partnership

Johns Hopkins-India connection

Giving back to his alma mater

Indian American physician and philanthropist Dr. Navin C. Shah has committed $525,000 to establish an infectious disease program at his alma mater, BJ Government Medical College in Pune, Maharashtra, in collaboration with Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.The five-year initiative, named the Navin C. Shah Infectious Disease Program, will support research, medical education, faculty and student exchanges, and patient care, particularly benefiting underserved communities in Pune.The agreement was signed at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, with Shah and Dr. Amita Gupta, the Florence Sabin Professor of Infectious Diseases and director of the Division of Infectious Diseases at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, participating in the ceremony.Gupta, who is also the founder and faculty co-chair of the Johns Hopkins India Institute, has been involved in infectious disease research and medical collaborations in India for more than two decades.The initiative represents a significant philanthropic investment in a longstanding academic partnership between Johns Hopkins and BJ Government Medical College, one of Pune’s major public medical institutions.“The purpose is to help my medical school in training, education, research and patient care as far as ID (infectious diseases) is concerned,” Shah, a resident of Potomac, MD, told The American Bazaar after the signing ceremony.For Shah, who grew up in Pune and graduated from BJ Government Medical College, the initiative is both a professional commitment and a personal effort to give back to the institution that shaped his medical career.“I grew up in Pune, so it is a win-win situation for me because not only my medical college will be benefited in the training, education, research and patient care, but other people, other hospitals which are treating poor patients in Pune will be benefited,” he said.The new program will focus on infectious diseases that continue to pose major public health challenges in India, including tuberculosis, HIV and infections resistant to commonly used antibiotics.In an interview with The American Bazaar, Gupta said Johns Hopkins researchers have been working with BJ Government Medical College since 2003 on a broad range of infectious disease projects.“The work that we do includes right from research to new treatments for TB, for HIV, for highly drug-resistant infections in adults and in children and pregnant women,” she said.The collaboration also encompasses medical education, training for doctors and nurses, and exchanges involving students and faculty from Johns Hopkins and institutions in Pune.Gupta emphasized the importance of BJ Government Medical College’s role in serving economically disadvantaged patients.“BJ Medical College is well known for really being the public hospital taking care of the poorest of the poor in Pune,” she said.The new funding will help expand activities that may not be adequately covered by conventional research grants.A patient care fund will also be established to support treatment and related needs.Gupta said the gift would support research, education and patient care over the five-year period, allowing the institutions to pursue additional opportunities beyond their existing projects.The program is also expected to strengthen the exchange of medical expertise between India and the United States.According to Shah, the arrangement will include visits by four Johns Hopkins faculty members to India and two BJ Government Medical College faculty members to the United States, along with exchanges involving students and medical residents.The initiative will also support an annual seminar bringing together medical experts from Pune and elsewhere in India.Shah said a seminar is scheduled to begin December 4, providing an early opportunity for specialists to share knowledge and discuss advances in infectious disease treatment.The Maryland urologist noted that the college’s affiliated hospital has approximately 1,800 beds and serves large numbers of patients from economically disadvantaged backgrounds.The new initiative builds on a relationship between Johns Hopkins researchers and Pune-based medical institutions that began with research into preventing HIV transmission from mothers to their children.During the signing ceremony, Gupta recalled arriving at Johns Hopkins in 2003, attracted in part by the opportunity to work in India.She credited Dr. Robert Bollinger, a Johns Hopkins physician and researcher, with helping establish early collaborations involving BJ Medical College and India’s National AIDS Research Institute.One of the initial projects examined the use of nevirapine to reduce mother-to-child HIV transmission.Over the years, the research partnership expanded considerably.“We’re looking at new TB drugs, TB vaccine, diagnostics, taking care of HIV, looking at drug resistant infections,” Gupta said during the ceremony.She noted that researchers had also studied dengue and health conditions such as diabetes and alcohol misuse that can complicate the treatment of patients with infectious diseases.Beyond research, Gupta described the partnership as a two-way learning experience for physicians, scientists and students.She said her work in Pune had allowed Johns Hopkins faculty to learn from Indian colleagues and patients while giving American medical professionals opportunities to participate in collaborative research.Philanthropic contributions, she explained, provide flexibility that conventional grant funding often lacks.Such support allows researchers to pursue innovative ideas, expand educational opportunities and strengthen patient services.“Without the sort of gratitude and the support of philanthropists such as yourself and your family, you know, much of what we do, we go hand to mouth with our grants,” she told Shah.The gift, she added, would enable the collaborators to be more creative and innovative in their work.Gupta also said she planned to travel to Pune for a December 3 inauguration associated with Shah’s contribution.The initiative comes as Johns Hopkins continues expanding its academic and research engagement with India through the Johns Hopkins India Institute.Gupta said the institute was created to bring together researchers and academic programs that had previously operated largely independently across the university.Its goal is to strengthen collaboration across disciplines and connect Johns Hopkins faculty with Indian universities, hospitals, government agencies and nonprofit organizations.Among its initiatives are a TB-free schools program, a fellowship supporting young women scientists in India, and collaborative research grants covering areas such as artificial intelligence in healthcare, medical education and public health.Gupta said Johns Hopkins’ India-related research and collaborative activities have involved approximately $80 million over the past decade.The new Pune initiative will become part of this broader network while retaining a specific focus on infectious diseases, medical training and patient care.Gupta also expressed hope that Shah’s contribution would encourage other alumni of BJ Government Medical College and members of the Indian diaspora to support healthcare and education in India.“One of the goals of his gift is to really get other alumni from BJ Medical College or those who care about Pune and more and then throughout India to be able to be generous with their philanthropic giving,” she said.Shah, a founder of the American Association of Physicians of Indian Origin (AAPI), has long been associated with efforts to connect Indian American medical professionals with healthcare initiatives in India.His latest commitment reflects the continuing role of Indian American physicians in supporting medical education and healthcare institutions in their country of origin.For Shah, the decision to fund the infectious disease program was driven by his connection to Pune and his belief that international medical partnerships can improve healthcare delivery.He hopes the program will strengthen the ability of BJ Government Medical College and other Pune hospitals to diagnose, study and treat infectious diseases.Gupta sees the collaboration in similarly broad terms.“I always look at it as it’s a bilateral partnership. Truly we learn and we give,” she said.“The world is a much better and safer place and a more productive and innovative place if we are working together across our geographies and our disciplines.”For BJ Government Medical College, the initiative promises additional resources, international expertise and opportunities for medical professionals to participate in research and training.For Shah, it marks a return to his roots through an investment in the institution where his medical journey began.“So education, training, research and patient care,” he said, summarizing his expectations for the program. “Hopefully my college, with the help of Hopkins, will improve in ID treatment, infectious disease treatment.”The urologist said the current funding would be distributed over five years, with an annual contribution of $105,000.Shah also indicated that his family might consider extending its support beyond the initial five-year commitment, potentially expanding the initiative to include kidney and lung diseases.At the signing ceremony, Shah was accompanied by his daughter, Shefali Shah, and his son, Dr. Amit Shah, who is also a physician.(By arrangement with The American Bazaar
Article Summary: Indian American physician and philanthropist Dr. Navin C. Shah has committed $525,000 to establish an infectious disease program at his alma mater, BJ Government Medical College in Pune, Maharashtra. The five-year initiative will support research, medical education, faculty and student exchanges, and patient care. The new program will focus on infectious diseases that continue to pose major public health challenges in India.

Article Title: A festival, a DJ and a complaint: What residents can legally do about noise
Article Text:
​From religious processions to weddings: When celebrations become a noise concern

From religious processions to weddings: When celebrations become a noise concern

How loud is too loud? What India's noise pollution rules say

Nighttime limits are lower than daytime limits across all four categories.

When a complaint about noise turns fatal

How loud is too loud?

What prolonged exposure to loud music can do to the body

A death during a loud celebration does not, by itself, establish that noise caused it. Medical evidence and proof of a legally sufficient causal link are crucial.

From police complaints to court action: What residents can legally do against noise violations

When can you complaint?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A DJ blaring past midnight, speakers drowning out conversations, or a celebration that leaves an entire neighbourhood awake- when does public celebration become a violation of the law?For residents, the choice can be difficult: put up with the noise or confront the organisers, sometimes risking a dispute with neighbours or those conducting the event.India has rules governing permissible noise levels, the use of loudspeakers and the hours during which they can operate. But knowing the rules and getting them enforced are two different things. What can residents do when repeated requests to turn down the volume go unheard? Can they call the police, file a formal complaint or take legal action against those responsible?Amplified music is a common feature of public celebrations across India, from religious processions and community festivals to weddings, political rallies and DJ nights. But when powerful speakers, heavy bass and prolonged performances spill into residential neighbourhoods, celebrations can become a source of distress for those living nearby.The concern is not the occasion itself, but the volume, duration and timing of the noise.Religious processions across communities may involve loudspeakers, music and sound systems. Ganeshotsav and Durga Puja immersion processions, for instance, may feature truck-mounted DJ systems, while Eid and Milad processions can also use amplified music and public-address systems, depending on local practices.Similar concerns can arise around other religious gatherings when loudspeakers operate close to homes, hospitals or educational institutions.Weddings and private parties are another frequent source of complaints, with DJs and live bands performing at banquet halls, open lawns and neighbourhood venues. Political rallies, election victory processions, concerts and commercial events can also generate sustained noise, particularly when sound systems are used in densely populated areas or late into the night.The consequences can extend beyond temporary discomfort. Prolonged or excessive noise can disrupt sleep and increase stress, and may be particularly distressing for infants, older people, patients and those who work night shifts. Heavy bass and vibrations can also travel into nearby homes, making it difficult for residents to escape the disturbance even indoors.India's noise pollution rules are governed by the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The rules distinguish between daytime, from 6am to 10pm, and nighttime, from 10pm to 6am, and prescribe different permissible ambient noise levels for industrial, commercial, residential and silence zones.The prescribed limits are 75 decibels during the day and 70 decibels at night in industrial areas; 65 and 55 decibels in commercial areas; 55 and 45 decibels in residential areas; and 50 and 40 decibels in silence zones, respectively. Silence zones may be notified around sensitive locations such as hospitals, educational institutions and courts, subject to applicable rules and notifications.The rules generally prohibit the use of loudspeakers between 10pm and 6am, subject to limited exemptions.Under Rule 5(3) of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, state governments may permit loudspeakers to be used between 10pm and midnight on specified cultural, religious or festive occasions for a maximum of 15 days in a calendar year, subject to conditions. The exemption is not automatic: the relevant dates must generally be specified in advance, and the permission remains subject to applicable conditions.However, the existence of prescribed limits does not always prevent violations. High-powered sound systems, late-night DJ performances and prolonged processions can become sources of complaints when noise levels exceed the applicable limits or loudspeakers are used without the necessary permissions.For residents, the challenge is often getting authorities to act when requests to lower the volume fail. In some cases, disputes over noise have escalated into confrontations, with fatal consequences.A request to turn down the volume should not become a matter of life and death. Yet, several reported incidents across India have highlighted how objections to loud music and late-night noise can escalate into violence. In some cases, people have allegedly been assaulted after confronting those responsible for the disturbance. In others, deaths have occurred during celebrations, prompting families to allege that excessive sound played a role.In an incident in Noida, Satish Sharma, a 45-year-old paying guest accommodation operator in Sector 93's Gejha area, died on September 4 following a confrontation over a loud home theatre system. Reports said he was chased and pushed onto the pavement during the altercation. Two brothers were arrested on charges of culpable homicide.Other reported incidents have raised concerns about medical emergencies during loud celebrations, including cases involving children.In Balrampur, Uttar Pradesh, seven-year-old Vaishnavi Tiwari reportedly collapsed in her classroom and died in September 2026 while a Ganesh immersion procession featuring a loud DJ system was passing outside the school. Reports said the DJ operator and owner were arrested in connection with the case. The precise cause of death and whether sound exposure played any role require confirmation from medical and investigative findings.In Sitamarhi district of Bihar, a groom reportedly collapsed and died during his wedding after complaining about loud DJ music and discomfort from speakers positioned nearby. Reports attributed his death to a heart attack, but whether noise exposure contributed to the medical emergency would need to be established through medical evidence.In another reported incident in Siddharthnagar, Uttar Pradesh, a two-day-old newborn died in October 2026 during an idol immersion procession accompanied by loud DJ music outside the family's home. The child's father alleged that the sound was extremely loud, that a projection roof outside the house partially collapsed and that the baby became unresponsive following a sudden burst of noise.The circumstances in these cases differ significantly. While some involve alleged assaults following objections to noise, others involve deaths during events where families have raised concerns about loud music.Prolonged exposure to high-decibel noise can trigger a physiological stress response, affecting heart rate, blood pressure and sleep. The health effects depend on the intensity and duration of exposure, as well as an individual's existing health conditions.“Loud noise is a biological alarm. Cortisol and adrenaline rise, heart rate and blood pressure spike, and the body cannot differentiate a DJ from a threat,” said Dr Mounica Vadlamudi, longevity physician and founder of BluPrint Longevity.Noise exposure may be particularly concerning for people with existing cardiovascular conditions. “Noise rarely creates a cardiac emergency from nothing, but it can tip a vulnerable heart over the edge,” Vadlamudi said, adding that WHO-commissioned research has linked chronic noise exposure to a higher risk of heart disease and hypertension.The risk of hearing damage depends on both sound intensity and the duration of exposure. Citing US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) guidance, Vadlamudi said exposure to 85 decibels for eight hours is the recommended occupational limit, with permissible exposure time halving for every 3-decibel increase. At 100 decibels, that works out to about 15 minutes under this standard.The impact can also extend to people who are not attending an event but live nearby. Loud music can disrupt sleep, affecting recovery and overall health over time. Highlighting the importance of protecting sleep as well as hearing Vadlamudi said one does not necessarily need to be close to the speaker “to pay the price”.Residents affected by excessively loud music can complain to the police and the authorities responsible for enforcing noise pollution rules. If their complaints go unanswered, they can escalate the matter to senior police officers, the district administration or pollution control authorities, and approach the courts to seek enforcement.Advocate Rupali Jain said residents should call 112, record the disturbance through videos and, where possible, sound-level readings, and preserve complaint numbers and records of the action taken. If the police fail to respond, they can approach senior police officers, the sub-divisional magistrate or the relevant pollution control authority.Advocate Pritish Sunil Teckchandani said residents could seek intervention under Section 152 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which provides for conditional orders to remove certain public nuisances. They can also approach the relevant pollution control board. If authorities repeatedly fail to enforce the rules, residents may move the High Court under Article 226, seeking directions to ensure compliance with noise regulations and relevant court orders.The legal consequences can be more serious when excessive noise is alleged to have contributed to a death. Jain said a family could seek registration of a case under Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide. Whether the provision applies would depend on evidence establishing negligence and a legally sufficient causal link between the noise and the death.“Causation is the crux,” Jain said, explaining that medical evidence is essential to establish whether noise contributed to a death. A post-mortem report and expert medical opinion, alongside available sound-level measurements, video recordings, witness statements and medical records, could help investigators assess the circumstances.A pre-existing medical condition would not automatically rule out a claim, but the extent to which noise aggravated the condition and contributed to the death would need to be established. Depending on the circumstances, families may also explore a civil claim for damages. Criminal prosecution or compensation is not automatic merely because a death occurred during a loud procession or celebration.Advocate Sumit Nagpal said DJ operators, event organisers and others responsible for a sound system could face legal consequences if the evidence established their liability. “Liability depends on proof of duty, breach, and causal contribution of the noise,” he said.Families who believe officials ignored repeated noise complaints can submit written representations to senior police officers and the district administration. They may also approach the High Court seeking directions to enforce the law and, where legally justified, pursue appropriate relief. Records of emergency calls, written complaints, complaint numbers and official responses can help establish whether authorities had prior notice of the disturbance. However, failure to respond does not by itself establish criminal liability on the part of an official.Jain said enforcement remained a major challenge despite existing regulations. “The law is adequate; enforcement is not,” she said, pointing to stretched police resources during festivals, limited decibel-monitoring equipment, low fines and sensitivities surrounding religious and political gatherings.Teckchandani also highlighted enforcement gaps, including the difficulty of monitoring simultaneous events, shortages of equipment and trained personnel, and reluctance to act against influential organisers. Better access to calibrated sound-monitoring equipment, effective complaint-handling systems and accountability for officials who ignore documented violations could help improve implementation.For residents, the available remedies range from documenting a violation and filing a complaint to seeking a magistrate’s intervention or approaching the High Court. Preserving evidence and escalating complaints through the appropriate channels can be critical when repeated violations go unchecked.The question is not simply how much noise is too much, but whether authorities enforce the law before a disturbance escalates into a confrontation or puts public health at risk.
Article Summary: India has rules governing permissible noise levels, the use of loudspeakers and the hours during which they can operate. Prolonged or excessive noise can disrupt sleep and increase stress, and may be particularly distressing for infants, older people, patients and those who work night shifts. Heavy bass and vibrations can also travel into nearby homes, making it difficult for residents to escape the disturbance.

Article Title: ‘Give priority to local artisans’: PM Modi’s festive shopping appeal as Diwali approaches
Article Text:
File photo: PM Modi

PM Modi stresses packaging, highlights traditional skills

Heval river rejuvenation , e-Sanjeevani consultations highlighted

PM calls 12-year journey of Mann Ki Baat a ‘pilgrimage’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday urged people to prioritise products made by local artisans while shopping for festivals, saying their purchases would strengthen the ‘Vocal for Local’ campaign and help realise the vision of a self-reliant India.Addressing the 139th edition of his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat , PM Modi said the campaign was helping Indian products reach international markets, citing the export of makhana from Bihar to Greece and arhar dal from Karnataka to the Maldives.The prime minister noted that people typically purchase gifts and other items for their families and loved ones during festivals, and called on them to support local artisans through their shopping choices.“This time too, while shopping, please give priority to products made by local artisans. Your purchases will boost their enthusiasm,” he said.PM Modi said greater participation in the ‘Vocal for Local’ campaign would accelerate the progress towards a self-reliant India.“Therefore, I personally urge you to give priority and prominence to products crafted by local artisans,” he added.The prime minister also emphasised the importance of packaging in attracting consumers and helping products find a place in the market.“Often, when we see something in the market, good packaging makes us pick it up, and we want to learn more about the product. Understanding this, greater emphasis is now being laid on packaging,” he said.During the broadcast, PM Modi also highlighted efforts to revive traditional skills and farming practices, including an initiative to promote natural cotton cultivation in Punjab’s Malwa region.He said the organisation Kheti Virasat Mission had been working to revive organic farming and had launched an initiative called ‘Nav-Trinjan’ to encourage natural cotton farming.The initiative also started a weaving school a few years ago to pass the traditional skill on to younger generations.“You can imagine how great a help this is for the environment. Friends, a few years ago, 'Nav-Trinjan' also started a weaving school with the goal of passing on the skill of weaving to the new generation,” PM Modi said.PM Modi also spoke about efforts by residents and the local administration in Uttarakhand’s Tehri Garhwal district to revive the Heval river.He said the river’s water level had begun to fall some time ago, while natural water sources in the surrounding areas were drying up. In response, villagers and the administration launched conservation efforts that included rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge and large-scale tree planting.“Today, these efforts have given the Heval river a new lease of life while also helping rejuvenate dozens of natural water sources,” the prime minister said.He also highlighted the use of technology in healthcare through the e-Sanjeevani telemedicine service, which enables people to access medical consultations remotely.“It brings me immense satisfaction to share that nearly 50 crore tele-consultations have been conducted through it so far. This is a massive figure and a prime example of the power of technology, the service-mindedness of our doctors, and the trust of our citizens,” he said.PM Modi added that the service’s extensive network enabled it to reach even the most remote parts of the country, with beneficiaries’ experiences offering examples of its reach.The Sunday broadcast also marked 12 years of Mann Ki Baat. PM Modi described the programme’s journey as a “pilgrimage”, saying it had allowed him to learn about citizens’ efforts and acknowledge their contributions.“Since then, our journey has been continuing without interruption. You are both fellow travellers and guides on this journey,” he said, recalling that the programme began on Vijayadashami 12 years ago.The prime minister said the broadcast had given him an opportunity to highlight the hard work, courage, dedication and spirit of service shown by ordinary people across the country.“For me, Mann Ki Baat is no less than a pilgrimage to closely learn about the efforts of the people of the country and to bow down to their contributions,” he said.PM Modi added that the programme had brought attention to people whose work might otherwise go unnoticed and had allowed him to connect with families across India.He said he received hundreds of messages from listeners who told him that listening to Mann Ki Baat made them feel as though he were sitting among them and speaking as a member of their family. NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday announced a major crackdown on an international narcotics cartel, with Operation Trident targeting 38 locations across Assam, Mizoram and Manipur.The operation, that took place on October 23, uncovered hawala transactions worth Rs 100 crore and resulted in the freezing of 1,424 bank accounts and the attachment of properties valued at Rs 17.82 crore. Officials also seized 500 detonators and Rs 12 lakh in cash, while 18 people were arrested.Announcing the operation on X, Shah said that the cartel was trafficking narcotics across India, Myanmar and Bangladesh through the Death Triangle Corridor. Article Title: No EC nod needed for voter to sue candidate over false information: Supreme Court
Article Text:
The Supreme Court said that Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act in 2002.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A voter can now not only cast a vote in an election but can also drag an election candidate to court and initiate criminal proceedings for lying and furnishing a false declaration as Supreme Court has ruled that a complaint filed by a private person alleging an offence under Section 125-A of Representation of People Act (filing false affidavit) is maintainable and the Election Commission’s nod was not needed.Explaining the interplay between Section 125-A of Representation of People Act and Section 195(1) of the CrPC which says that no court shall take cognisance of any offences punishable under sections 172 to 188, including the offence of furnishing false information to a public servant, the top court held that Section 125A of RoP Act does not come within the ambit of Section 195 of CrPC and a court can take cognisance of a private complaint. The court’s ruling will further empower the electorate against candidates who lied in their affidavits.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed the Karnataka HC order which had held that “right given to the voter is only to file an election petition, and not to register a private complaint of crime which is the duty of the Election Commission, if it wants to do so”.SC said that Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act in 2002, while Section 195 of CrPC was amended in 2006, and that the omission of the legislature to include Section 125-A of the RoP Act in Section 195 of CrPC was deliberate and no court would be barred from taking cognisance of an alleged offence under Section 125-A of the RoP Act, even on the complaint lodged by a private person.“Should we read into Section 195 of CrPC a prohibition in respect of Section 125-A of the RoP Act also, apart from those expressly included? If indeed it were the intention of the legislature that cognisance of any offence relating to furnishing of false information by a candidate in an affidavit with intent of being elected in an election (referred to in Section 125-A of the RoP Act) could only be taken if the complainant were a public servant, the same could have been provided by an amendment of Section 195, CrPC since Section 125-A of the RoP Act is of fairly recent origin. ”SC also refused to give credence to the EC’s press note that it can take cognisance of such complaints and refer such matters to the relevant investigating authorities on a case-to-case basis. “...Even though the ECI is supreme in its own sphere and has, indeed, issued guidelines/press notes based on its understanding of the statutory provisions, interpretation of statutes is primarily the task of the courts and such guidelines/press notes do not bind us,” the court said.It said that Karnataka HC erred in holding that a private complaint cannot be filed for an offence under Section 125A of RoP Act which is punishable up to six months of jail term. The HC had interpreted the provision solely upon reading the letter issued by the Election Commission of India on the issue which was rejected by the apex court.Allaying the apprehension that allowing the lodging of a criminal complaint by a private person would be misused and frivolous cases would be filed by political rivals, SC said, “If at all a complaint is lodged to harass an elected candidate or frivolous allegations are levelled therein, the laws of the country duly empower the competent magistrates to pass such order(s) as they deem fit and proper commensurate with the facts and circumstances of each case. ”
Article Summary: Supreme Court has ruled that a complaint filed by a private person alleging an offence under Section 125-A of Representation of People Act (filing false affidavit) is maintainable. The court’s ruling will further empower the electorate against candidates who lied in their affidavits.

Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.
